name: Git & GitHub
description: Git tracks every change to your code, and GitHub lets you share it and work together with a team.

topics.title: What is Git? Install and Setup

blocks.html:
What is Git? Install and Setup

What is Git?

Git is a version control system. It watches the files in a project folder and remembers every change you save, like an unlimited "undo" history for your whole project. Each saved moment is called a commit. If you break something on Tuesday, you can go back to how the project looked on Monday.

Git also helps teams. Five students can work on the same project at the same time, and Git combines their work. Without it, people end up with folders named final, final2 and final-REAL.

Git and GitHub are not the same thing. Git is a free program that runs on your own computer. GitHub is a website that stores Git projects online so you can share them. You can use Git without GitHub, but not GitHub without Git.

Install and Configure Git

Download Git from git-scm.com and install it with the default options. Then open a terminal (on Windows, use Git Bash) and check that it works with git --version.

Before your first commit, tell Git who you are. Your name and email are stored in every commit you make. You only do this once per computer, using git config --global. We also set main as the default branch name for new projects.

blocks.code:
git --version
git config --global user.name "Sara Ahmed"
git config --global user.email "sara@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global --list
blocks.output:
git version 2.43.0
user.name=Sara Ahmed
user.email=sara@example.com
init.defaultbranch=main

blocks.html: Your version number will be different, and that is fine. Notice that Git prints the setting name init.defaultbranch in lowercase when it lists them.

Your First Repository

A repository (or "repo") is a project folder that Git is tracking. Go inside a folder and run git init. Git creates a hidden folder called .git. This is where Git keeps the whole history. Never edit or delete it by hand: if you delete .git, the history is gone and the folder is just a normal folder again.

blocks.code:
mkdir notes
cd notes
git init
ls -a
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/notes/.git/
.
..
.git

blocks.html:
The Three Areas

The most important idea in Git is that your files live in three areas. A change moves from left to right in two small steps.

AreaWhat it isCommand to move on
Working directoryThe real files you editgit add
Staging areaA waiting room: changes you chose for the next commitgit commit
RepositoryThe saved history inside .git(done)

Why a staging area? It lets you choose exactly which changes go into a commit. You can edit five files and commit only two of them. In the demo below, git status --short shows ?? for a new file Git does not know yet, and A for a file that is staged. Real hashes such as a1b2c3d will be different on your computer, because each commit gets its own unique ID.

blocks.code:
echo "Git keeps my history" > hello.txt
git status --short
git add hello.txt
git status --short
git commit -m "Add hello.txt"
git status --short
blocks.output:
?? hello.txt
A  hello.txt
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add hello.txt
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 hello.txt

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Running git init in the wrong place, such as your whole Documents or Desktop folder. Always cd into the project folder first.
  • Forgetting to set user.name and user.email. Git will complain or guess a wrong name.
  • Thinking that saving a file in your editor is the same as committing. Saving only changes the working directory.
  • Mixing up Git and GitHub.

Key Points

  • Git is a version control system that runs on your computer; GitHub is a website for sharing Git projects.
  • Set your name and email once with git config --global.
  • git init turns a folder into a repository by creating the hidden .git folder.
  • Files move from working directory to staging area (git add) to repository (git commit).
  • Commit IDs (hashes) are unique, so yours will not match the ones in these demos.

Your First Commit

The Everyday Loop

Almost all daily Git work is a small loop: change files, check status, add, commit. Learn this loop well and you already know most of Git.

  1. Edit or create files in your project.
  2. git status shows what changed.
  3. git add moves chosen changes to the staging area.
  4. git commit -m "message" saves them to the history.

git status is the command you will run most. Use it all the time. It never changes anything, and it always tells you what to do next. Start with a new, empty repository.

blocks.code:
mkdir todo-app
cd todo-app
git init
git status
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/todo-app/.git/
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)

blocks.html:
Add and Status

Now create two files. Git sees them but does not track them yet, so they are listed as untracked. Then stage only README.md with git add README.md. Look at how git status now shows two groups: "Changes to be committed" (staged) and "Untracked files" (not staged).

You can stage everything with git add .. The dot means "this folder and everything inside it". It is quick, but check git status first so you do not add files by accident.

blocks.code:
echo "# Todo App" > README.md
echo "console.log('todo');" > app.js
git status
git add README.md
git status
blocks.output:
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	README.md
	app.js

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	app.js

blocks.html:
Committing

A commit is a snapshot of everything in the staging area, together with your name, the date and a message. Use -m to write the message on the command line. Git prints the branch name, a short hash, and a summary of the changes. Finally git log --oneline shows the history, newest commit first.

blocks.code:
git commit -m "Add README with project title"
git add app.js
git commit -m "Add app.js entry file"
git log --oneline
blocks.output:
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add README with project title
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md
[main b2c3d4e] Add app.js entry file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 app.js
b2c3d4e Add app.js entry file
a1b2c3d Add README with project title

blocks.html:
Writing Good Commit Messages

Months later, the message is the only thing that tells you why a commit exists. Make it useful.

Weak messageBetter message
fixFix crash when the todo list is empty
changesAdd delete button to todo items
asdfUpdate README with install steps
  • Keep the first line short, about 50 characters.
  • Start with a verb: Add, Fix, Update, Remove.
  • Describe what the commit does. One commit should do one job.

Common Mistakes

  • Committing without git add. Git says "nothing added to commit" because the staging area is empty.
  • Editing a file after git add and forgetting that the new edit is not staged. Run git add again.
  • Making one huge commit at the end of the week. Commit small and often.

Key Points

  • The loop is: edit, git status, git add, git commit -m.
  • New files are untracked until you add them.
  • A commit saves only what is staged.
  • git log --oneline shows a short history.
  • Write short messages that start with a verb and say what changed.

History and Undoing Things

Looking at History

Git remembers everything, so you can look back at any time. git log shows full details, and git log --oneline shows one short line per commit. Let us build a small project with two commits.

blocks.code:
mkdir shop
cd shop
git init
echo "price = 100" > price.txt
git add price.txt
git commit -m "Add price"
echo "price = 120" >> price.txt
git commit -am "Add second price"
git log --oneline
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/shop/.git/
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add price
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 price.txt
[main b2c3d4e] Add second price
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
b2c3d4e Add second price
a1b2c3d Add price

blocks.html:
Seeing Changes with git diff

git diff shows what you changed but have not staged yet. Lines starting with + were added and lines starting with - were removed. (git diff --staged shows the staged changes.)

To throw away a mistake, use git restore. There are two kinds:

  • git restore file discards your edits in the working directory and brings back the last committed version.
  • git restore --staged file only removes the file from the staging area. Your edits stay in the file.

Be careful: git restore file deletes your uncommitted edits for good. Git cannot bring them back, because they were never saved in a commit.

blocks.code:
echo "price = 999" >> price.txt
git diff
git restore price.txt
cat price.txt
echo "oops" >> price.txt
git add price.txt
git status --short
git restore --staged price.txt
git status --short
git restore price.txt
blocks.output:
diff --git a/price.txt b/price.txt
index c3d4e5f..d4e5f6a 100644
--- a/price.txt
+++ b/price.txt
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 price = 100
 price = 120
+price = 999
price = 100
price = 120
M  price.txt
 M price.txt

blocks.html:
Undoing a Commit: revert

What if the bad change is already committed? The safest tool is git revert. It creates a new commit that does the opposite of an old one. The old commit stays in the history, so nothing is lost. This is the right choice for work you have already shared with other people.

In this demo the revert prints a Date: line. Yours will show your own date and time.

blocks.code:
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log --oneline
cat price.txt
blocks.output:
[main e5f6a7b] Revert "Add second price"
 Date: Mon Jan 5 10:30:00 2026 +0500
 1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
e5f6a7b Revert "Add second price"
b2c3d4e Add second price
a1b2c3d Add price
price = 100

blocks.html:
Undoing a Commit: reset

git reset moves the branch back to an older commit, as if the newer commits never happened. HEAD means "the commit I am on now", and HEAD~1 means "one commit before that".

CommandWhat happens to your files
git reset --soft HEAD~1Commit removed; changes stay staged
git reset HEAD~1Commit removed; changes stay in files, not staged (the default, called mixed)
git reset --hard HEAD~1Commit removed and changes deleted

The demo uses --hard to remove a wrong commit completely.

blocks.code:
echo "price = 500" >> price.txt
git commit -am "Wrong price"
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git log --oneline
blocks.output:
[main f6a7b8c] Wrong price
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
HEAD is now at e5f6a7b Revert "Add second price"
e5f6a7b Revert "Add second price"
b2c3d4e Add second price
a1b2c3d Add price

blocks.html:
Which Undo Should I Use?

  • Edit not committed yet: git restore.
  • Commit already shared with others: git revert.
  • Commit only on your computer and you want it gone: git reset.

Warning: git reset --hard destroys uncommitted work. Do not use it on commits you have already pushed to a shared repository.

Key Points

  • git log --oneline lists the history in short form.
  • git diff shows unstaged changes: + for added lines, - for removed lines.
  • git restore file discards edits; git restore --staged file unstages.
  • git revert adds a new commit that cancels an old one; it is safe for shared work.
  • git reset --hard rewrites history and deletes changes; use it with care.

Branches and Merging

What is a Branch?

A branch is a separate line of work. Imagine you want to build a login page, but the main project must keep working. You create a branch, build the login page there, and only when it is ready do you bring it back into the main line. If your experiment fails, you delete the branch and nothing is harmed.

The default branch is called main. A branch in Git is very cheap: it is only a small pointer to a commit, so you can make as many as you like.

CommandMeaning
git branchList branches (the star marks the current one)
git branch nameCreate a branch
git switch nameMove to a branch
git switch -c nameCreate a branch and move to it
git merge nameBring that branch into the current one
git branch -d nameDelete a merged branch

blocks.code:
mkdir site
cd site
git init
echo "Home page" > index.txt
git add index.txt
git commit -m "Add home page"
git branch
git switch -c feature-login
git branch
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/site/.git/
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add home page
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 index.txt
* main
Switched to a new branch 'feature-login'
* feature-login
  main

blocks.html:
Fast-Forward Merge

Now make a commit on feature-login, go back to main and merge. Look at ls before and after. When you switch branches, Git changes the files in your folder to match that branch, so login.txt is missing on main until you merge.

Because main had no new commits of its own, Git only has to move the main pointer forward. This is called a fast-forward merge. No new commit is needed.

blocks.code:
echo "Login page" > login.txt
git add login.txt
git commit -m "Add login page"
git switch main
ls
git merge feature-login
ls
blocks.output:
[feature-login b2c3d4e] Add login page
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 login.txt
Switched to branch 'main'
index.txt
Updating a1b2c3d..b2c3d4e
Fast-forward
 login.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 login.txt
index.txt
login.txt

blocks.html:
Merge Commit

Sometimes both branches have new commits. Then Git cannot just move a pointer. It combines the two lines and creates a special merge commit that has two parents. In the demo, feature-footer and main each get a new commit, and the merge joins them. The graph from git log --oneline --graph shows the two lines splitting and joining again.

blocks.code:
git switch -c feature-footer
echo "Footer" > footer.txt
git add footer.txt
git commit -m "Add footer"
git switch main
echo "About page" > about.txt
git add about.txt
git commit -m "Add about page"
git merge feature-footer -m "Merge feature-footer"
git log --oneline --graph
blocks.output:
Switched to a new branch 'feature-footer'
[feature-footer c3d4e5f] Add footer
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 footer.txt
Switched to branch 'main'
[main d4e5f6a] Add about page
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 about.txt
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 footer.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 footer.txt
*   e5f6a7b Merge feature-footer
|\  
| * c3d4e5f Add footer
* | d4e5f6a Add about page
|/  
* b2c3d4e Add login page
* a1b2c3d Add home page

blocks.html:
Cleaning Up

After a merge, the branch has done its job. Delete it with git branch -d. The commits are not lost, because they are now part of main. Git refuses to delete a branch that is not merged yet, which protects you from mistakes.

blocks.code:
git branch -d feature-login feature-footer
git branch
blocks.output:
Deleted branch feature-login (was b2c3d4e).
Deleted branch feature-footer (was c3d4e5f).
* main

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Merging in the wrong direction. First switch to the branch that should receive the changes (usually main), then run git merge other-branch.
  • Making commits on main when you meant to be on a feature branch. Check with git branch or git status.
  • Switching branches with uncommitted changes. Commit or stash them first.

Key Points

  • A branch is a separate line of work; main is the default.
  • git switch -c name creates a branch and moves to it.
  • Merge from the receiving branch: git merge feature.
  • Fast-forward: only a pointer moves. Merge commit: both branches had new work.
  • Delete finished branches with git branch -d.

Merge Conflicts

Why Conflicts Happen

Git can merge two branches automatically when they change different files or different lines. A merge conflict happens when both branches changed the same lines of the same file in different ways. Git does not know which version is right, so it stops and asks you.

Conflicts are normal in team work. They are not an error and nothing is broken. Let us create one on purpose: one branch changes the greeting to "Hello Lahore", while main changes the same line to "Hello Pakistan".

blocks.code:
mkdir greeting
cd greeting
git init
echo "Hello World" > hello.txt
git add hello.txt
git commit -m "Add greeting"
git switch -c feature-lahore
echo "Hello Lahore" > hello.txt
git commit -am "Greet Lahore"
git switch main
echo "Hello Pakistan" > hello.txt
git commit -am "Greet Pakistan"
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/greeting/.git/
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add greeting
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 hello.txt
Switched to a new branch 'feature-lahore'
[feature-lahore b2c3d4e] Greet Lahore
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
Switched to branch 'main'
[main c3d4e5f] Greet Pakistan
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

blocks.html:
Conflict Markers

Now merge. Git reports the conflict, and git status --short shows UU, which means "both sides modified". Git writes both versions into the file between special markers:

MarkerMeaning
<<<<<<< HEADStart: your current branch version follows
=======Divider between the two versions
>>>>>>> feature-lahoreEnd: the incoming branch version came before this line

blocks.code:
git merge feature-lahore
git status --short
cat hello.txt
blocks.output:
Auto-merging hello.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in hello.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
UU hello.txt
<<<<<<< HEAD
Hello Pakistan
=======
Hello Lahore
>>>>>>> feature-lahore

blocks.html:
Resolving and Finishing the Merge

To resolve a conflict, follow these steps:

  1. Open the file and decide what the final text should be: keep one side, keep the other, or combine them.
  2. Delete all the marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>).
  3. Save the file, then run git add on it to say "this one is solved".
  4. Run git commit to finish the merge.

In the demo we combine both ideas into "Hello Lahore, Pakistan". The editor in VS Code also shows buttons such as "Accept Current Change" and "Accept Both Changes", which do the same edit for you.

blocks.code:
echo "Hello Lahore, Pakistan" > hello.txt
git add hello.txt
git commit -m "Merge feature-lahore"
git status
git log --oneline --graph
blocks.output:
[main d4e5f6a] Merge feature-lahore
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
*   d4e5f6a Merge feature-lahore
|\  
| * b2c3d4e Greet Lahore
* | c3d4e5f Greet Pakistan
|/  
* a1b2c3d Add greeting

blocks.html:
Common Mistakes

  • Committing the file while the markers are still inside it. The markers are plain text, so Git will happily save them and your code will break.
  • Forgetting git add after fixing the file. The merge is not finished until you add and commit.
  • Panicking. If it goes wrong, git merge --abort cancels the merge and takes you back to before it started.
  • Keeping branches alive for weeks. Merge often, so conflicts stay small.

Key Points

  • A conflict means both branches changed the same lines.
  • Git marks the file with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>.
  • Edit the file to the final text and remove every marker.
  • Finish with git add then git commit.
  • git merge --abort is your escape button.

.gitignore, Stash and Tags

Files Git Should Not Track

Some files should never go into your repository:

  • node_modules/: thousands of downloaded packages. Anyone can recreate them with npm install.
  • .env: your private settings, such as database passwords and API keys.
  • Build output, log files and editor settings.

Create a text file called .gitignore in the project folder and list one pattern per line. Git then pretends those files do not exist. A trailing slash (node_modules/) means a folder, and *.log matches every file ending in .log. You should commit the .gitignore file itself.

blocks.code:
mkdir webapp
cd webapp
git init
mkdir node_modules
echo "module code" > node_modules/pkg.js
echo "DB_PASSWORD=hunter2" > .env
echo "console.log('hi');" > app.js
git status --short
printf 'node_modules/\n.env\n' > .gitignore
git status --short
git check-ignore -v .env
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/webapp/.git/
?? .env
?? app.js
?? node_modules/
?? .gitignore
?? app.js
.gitignore:2:.env	.env

blocks.html:
Never Commit Secrets

Passwords, tokens and API keys must never be committed. Once a secret is in the history, anyone with access to the repository can read it, and on a public GitHub repository that means the whole world. Bots scan GitHub all day looking for leaked keys. Put secrets in a .env file, add .env to .gitignore before your first commit, and share a safe example file such as .env.example with fake values instead.

Also note that .gitignore only affects files Git is not tracking yet. If you already committed a file, ignoring it later does not remove it.

Stash: Save Work for Later

Imagine you are halfway through a feature when your teammate asks for a quick fix on main. Your work is not ready to commit. git stash puts your uncommitted changes in a safe drawer and gives you a clean folder. Later, git stash pop takes the changes out again.

blocks.code:
git add .
git commit -m "Add app and gitignore"
echo "console.log('half done');" >> app.js
git stash
git status --short
cat app.js
git stash list
blocks.output:
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add app and gitignore
 2 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 app.js
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: a1b2c3d Add app and gitignore
console.log('hi');
stash@{0}: WIP on main: a1b2c3d Add app and gitignore

blocks.code:
git stash pop
cat app.js
git stash list
blocks.output:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   app.js

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (b2c3d4e9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a09)
console.log('hi');
console.log('half done');

blocks.html:
CommandMeaning
git stashSave uncommitted changes and clean the folder
git stash listShow what is in the drawer
git stash popBring back the latest stash and remove it from the list

Tags: Name a Moment

A tag is a permanent name for one commit. People use tags for releases, such as v1.0. A plain tag is just a name. An annotated tag (with -a) also stores a message, the author and a date. In git log --oneline --decorate you can see the tags next to the commit they point to. To share tags with GitHub you push them with git push --tags.

blocks.code:
git commit -am "Finish feature"
git tag v1.0
git tag -a v1.1 -m "Second release"
git tag
git log --oneline --decorate
blocks.output:
[main c3d4e5f] Finish feature
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
v1.0
v1.1
c3d4e5f (HEAD -> main, tag: v1.1, tag: v1.0) Finish feature
a1b2c3d Add app and gitignore

blocks.html:
Key Points

  • .gitignore lists files and folders Git should leave alone, such as node_modules/ and .env.
  • Never commit passwords or keys. Ignore the file before the first commit.
  • Ignoring a file does not remove it if it is already tracked.
  • git stash hides unfinished work; git stash pop restores it.
  • git tag v1.0 marks a commit, for example a release.

GitHub and Remotes

What is a Remote?

So far everything lived on your computer. A remote is a copy of your repository stored somewhere else, usually on GitHub. It gives you a backup, and it lets teammates get your work. By tradition, the main remote is named origin.

To start: create an account on GitHub, click New repository, choose a name, and copy the repository URL. Then connect your local project to it. These are the main commands:

CommandWhat it does
git remote add origin URLGive the remote the name origin
git pushUpload your commits
git pullDownload new commits and merge them into your branch
git fetchDownload new commits but do not change your files
git clone URLCopy a whole remote repository to your computer

The demos below use a plain folder as the "remote" so they run without internet. A GitHub URL such as https://github.com/you/notes.git works in exactly the same way.

blocks.code:
git init --bare notes-remote.git
mkdir notes
cd notes
git init
echo "First note" > notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -m "Add first note"
git remote add origin ../notes-remote.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main
blocks.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/notes-remote.git/
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/notes/.git/
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add first note
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 notes.txt
origin	../notes-remote.git (fetch)
origin	../notes-remote.git (push)
To ../notes-remote.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

blocks.html:
Push, Clone and Pull

The -u in git push -u origin main links your local main to origin/main, so later you can type just git push or git pull. Now imagine a teammate. They clone the repository, add a note, and push it.

blocks.code:
cd ..
git clone notes-remote.git notes-copy
cd notes-copy
echo "Second note" >> notes.txt
git commit -am "Add second note"
git push
cd ../notes
blocks.output:
Cloning into 'notes-copy'...
done.
[main b2c3d4e] Add second note
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
To /home/student/notes-remote.git
   a1b2c3d..b2c3d4e  main -> main

blocks.html:
Fetch and Pull

Back in your own copy, git fetch downloads what is new but leaves your files alone. git status then says your branch is behind origin/main. git pull is a fetch followed by a merge, and it brings the new commit into your branch.

blocks.code:
git fetch
git status
git pull
cat notes.txt
blocks.output:
From ../notes-remote
   a1b2c3d..b2c3d4e  main       -> origin/main
On branch main
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 1 commit, and can be fast-forwarded.
  (use "git pull" to update your local branch)

nothing to commit, working tree clean
Updating a1b2c3d..b2c3d4e
Fast-forward
 notes.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
First note
Second note

blocks.html:
SSH or HTTPS?

GitHub gives you two kinds of URL. HTTPS URLs (https://github.com/...) are the easiest to start with, but GitHub no longer accepts your account password for Git operations: you must use a personal access token (a long password you create in your GitHub settings) or a credential helper that logs you in through the browser. SSH URLs (git@github.com:...) use a key pair: you create a key on your computer, upload the public half to GitHub once, and never type a password again. Either way is fine for a student.

Common Mistakes

  • Pushing before pulling. If a teammate pushed first, Git rejects your push. Run git pull, fix any conflicts, then push again.
  • Pasting your token or password into a file in the repository.
  • Thinking GitHub updates by itself. Your commits stay on your computer until you run git push.

Key Points

  • A remote is a copy of the repository on another machine; origin is the usual name.
  • git push uploads, git fetch downloads without merging, git pull downloads and merges.
  • git clone copies a repository and sets up origin for you.
  • Use git push -u origin main the first time.
  • HTTPS needs a token, not your password; SSH uses keys.

Pull Requests and Team Workflow

The Team Workflow

In a team, nobody commits straight to main. Instead, everyone follows the same steps, so the main branch always stays working.

  1. Fork or clone. On a project you do not own (open source), click Fork on GitHub to make your own copy, then clone it. In a team project you can usually clone the shared repository directly.
  2. Make a branch for each feature, with a clear name like feature-search.
  3. Commit and push your branch to GitHub.
  4. Open a pull request (PR) on GitHub.
  5. Review. Teammates read your changes, leave comments, and ask for fixes.
  6. Merge the PR into main once it is approved.

A pull request is a request that says: "I finished some work on this branch. Please review it and merge it into main." It is a GitHub feature, not a Git command. Here is the first part: a branch pushed to the shared repository.

blocks.code:
git init --bare team-repo.git
git clone team-repo.git me
cd me
echo "v1" > app.txt
git add app.txt
git commit -m "Start app"
git push -u origin main
git switch -c feature-search
echo "search" > search.txt
git add search.txt
git commit -m "Add search"
git push -u origin feature-search

blocks.html:
Keeping Your Branch Up to Date

While you work, teammates keep merging their features into main. Your branch slowly becomes old. Update it regularly with git fetch origin and then git merge origin/main, while you are on your feature branch. Any conflicts are solved the same way as before. This is much easier when you do it often. In this demo a teammate pushes a change to main and then we bring it into feature-search.

cd ..
git clone team-repo.git mate
cd mate
echo "v2" > app.txt
git commit -am "Update app text"
git push
cd ../me
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main

blocks.html:
Warning: Secrets in History

Suppose someone commits a password by mistake and then removes the file in the next commit. Is the password safe now? No. The old commit still exists. The demo shows that git show can print the deleted content straight from the history. If it was pushed to GitHub, other people (and bots) may already have copied it.

blocks.code:
git switch main
echo "DB_PASSWORD=hunter2" > .env
git add .env
git commit -m "Add env file"
git rm .env
git commit -m "Remove env file"
ls -a
git log --oneline -- .env
git show HEAD~1:.env

blocks.html: If a password or key is ever committed, rotate it. This means: log in to the service, make the old password or key invalid, and create a new one. Deleting the file is not enough. Removing a secret from the history is possible with special tools, but you must still treat the old secret as stolen.

Good PR Habits

  • Keep PRs small, with one purpose each.
  • Write a clear title and say what you changed and why.
  • Read your own changes on GitHub before asking others to review.
  • Be kind in reviews: comment on the code, not the person.
  • After the merge, delete the branch and update your local main with git pull.

Key Points

  • One branch per feature; never work directly on main in a team.
  • A pull request asks teammates to review a branch and merge it.
  • Fork when you do not own the repository.
  • Keep your branch current with git fetch and git merge origin/main.
  • A committed secret stays in history: rotate it, because deleting the file is not enough.
